new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress is fixed on the first syllable of the word, independent of syllable weight (vowel length or coda). Corroborated by the reference grammar (Feist 2015: 41 = thesis 2011: 47): 'Saami words are said to comprise one or more stress groups. A stress group is composed of at least one stressed syllable and may be followed by either one or two unstressed syllables. A word which contains more than three syllables will typically form more than one stress group, where odd syllables are stressed.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Per Korhonen et al. 1973 as reported by Miestamo: weak secondary stress on the last syllable; in words longer than two syllables medial syllables carry a stronger secondary stress; if a disyllable is followed by an overshort (non-syllabic) vowel the second syllable gets stronger secondary stress; certain case endings affect secondary stress on the preceding syllable. Korhonen 1975 (also via Miestamo): long vowels in non-first syllables always bear secondary stress; unstressed syllables are open with overshort vowels. Historically secondary stress fell on the 3rd, 5th.. syllable (trochaic; Korhonen 1975: 15, Sammallahti 1998: 39); Feist 2015: 41 states odd syllables are stressed within stress groups; Miestamo judges the present-day system to show no clear foot type (WALS 17 value 4).
new_statements.exceptions: None for primary stress; Miestamo states explicitly that first-syllable stress holds regardless of syllable weight. (Recent loanwords are not discussed with respect to stress in any opened source.)
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level primary stress; the Saamic 'stress group' (stressed syllable + 1-2 unstressed) is the unit of gradation/palatalisation in Feist. No phrase-level or citation-form caveats given. Miestamo p.116 also: 'Skolt Saami has no tones.' Variety: standard Skolt Saami of Finland (Sevettijärvi/Suonjel-based), as in Korhonen et al. 1973 and Feist 2015.
new_statements.identity_note: All opened sources describe the Skolt Saami of Finland (Sevettijärvi / former Suonjel-Suõʹnn'jel community, the basis of the written standard), glottocode skol1241; no separate treatment of the Neiden (Norway) or Notozero/Tuloma (Russia) dialects' stress.

sources.note: p.116 (WALS features 14-17): stress is on the first syllable, fixed, no weight-sensitivity (citing Korhonen et al. 1973: 23-24); secondary stress: weak on last syllable, stronger on medial syllables, modulated by overshort vowels and certain case endings; Korhonen 1975: long vowels always bear secondary stress; historically secondary stress on 3rd, 5th.. syllables (trochaic), present-day system shows no clear foot type; p.116 also 'Skolt Saami has no tones'.

sources.note: Ch.2 Phonology has no dedicated stress section; section 2.1 'Word structure' p.41 defines the stress group after Sammallahti (1998: 39): words comprise one or more stress groups, each beginning with a stressed syllable followed by one or two unstressed syllables; words of more than three syllables form several stress groups 'where odd syllables are stressed' (i.e. initial primary stress, alternating rhythm). p.101 defers prosodic correlates of quantity (pitch, intensity) to McRobbie-Utasi 1999. No other statement on word stress found (a full-text search for stress/accent).
